The Gripen F will now enter a more extensive test program, with its capabilities and payloads gradually expanded. The Gripen F is designed to be more than just a training aircraft. One of the most obvious future roles for the Gripen F could be controlling unmanned aircraft. Saab is already developing the low-observable, AI-powered Autonomous Collaborative Platform (ACP) loyal-wingman, which is intended to operate alongside Gripen fighters and GlobalEye airborne early warning and control aircraft (AEW&C).

headline: A recent incident in which a Ukrainian FP-1 long-range one-way attack drone was intercepted by a Su-30SM fighter using its GSh-30-1 30 mm autocannon shows the potential of 4++ generation fighters against small aerial targets. The Su-30SM’s N011M Bars-R radar uses a passive electronically scanned array. Although it is no longer considered a modern radar, it can detect targets with a radar cross-section of less than 0.05 m² at ranges of 35–50+ km against a ground or water background in relatively low-jamming conditions. The aircraft’s infrared search and track (IRST) system can also detect drones by their engine heat signature, although its range can be reduced in poor weather. A specialized X/Ku-band AESA radar carried by an Inokhodets-RU-type UAV could further improve this capability by providing longer-range detection and a wider field of view, allowing fighters to receive earlier targeting information. The interception also shows how Su-30SM fighters could help reduce the workload on ground-based air-defense systems when dealing with low-flying drones. With the increasing use of small UAVs with low radar and thermal signatures, upgrading fighter radars and electro-optical systems should become a priority. Modern sensor arrays and digital processors could improve detection and tracking ranges and increase the chances of successfully engaging these targets. One option would be to upgrade older fourth-generation and 4+ generation fighters, including the Su-30M2, Su-33, Su-27SM and MiG-29S/SMT, with more modern Irbis-E radars, similar to the U.S. F-15E upgrade with the AN/APG-82(V)1 radar. They could also receive OLS-35 Infrared Search and Track (IRST) systems, along with 101KS-N and T220 targeting pods. Another option would be to equip hundreds of these fighters with IRST systems and small guided S-8L rockets. This could provide a relatively cheap way to engage drones while reducing the use of more expensive air-to-air missiles and increasing the number of targets a fighter can engage. A system similar to the U.S. AGR-20F APKWS II could provide a low-cost guided weapon solution specifically for countering unmanned aerial systems.

headline: The Iran war is creating growing concerns about U.S. munitions inventories and the ability to respond to a major contingency involving China or Russia. According to U.S. officials cited by the Wall Street Journal, PAC-3 Patriot interceptors and ATACMS missiles in Europe have fallen to “beyond critical” levels. Other precision weapons and guided rockets have also been drawn down, while THAAD interceptors and counter-drone systems have been moved from Europe to the Middle East. By mid-July, U.S. forces had reportedly expended approximately 1,700 Patriot interceptors, 200 THAAD interceptors and 150 Navy Standard Missiles during the Iran conflict. Iran has launched more than 1,500 ballistic missiles and 6,000 large drones during the war. The depletion is affecting U.S. planning. European Command has reportedly adjusted operational plans, while officials have previously acknowledged that current inventories could constrain the ability to execute contingency plans for Taiwan. The problem is compounded by production timelines. Replenishing some advanced interceptors and missiles could take years, even as European allies face delays receiving weapons they have already purchased. The White House and Pentagon dispute the characterization of a broader U.S. munitions shortage, saying current inventories remain sufficient to meet America's strategic objectives. NATO likewise says the alliance retains enough air-defense munitions for its defense. headline: President Trump says the U.S. has secured majority control over a joint venture covering more than 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan oil reserves, following the administration’s effort to bring American energy companies back into Venezuela. Under the reported arrangement, Venezuela’s interim government granted the venture a 100-year concession to operate the affected oil fields. The U.S. government would control 55% of the venture, through a combination of equity and the ability to acquire oil at cost. The Trump administration says the arrangement could bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, increase U.S. oil supplies and eventually reduce energy prices. The administration also says the deal comes at no cost to U.S. taxpayers. The agreement covers roughly one-fifth of Venezuela’s more than 300 billion barrels of proven reserves. Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves, but production has been constrained for years by underinvestment, deteriorating infrastructure, sanctions and the nationalization of foreign-owned assets. The identity of the private operator involved in the joint venture has not yet been disclosed. Companies including Chevron, Repsol and Eni still have operations or interests in Venezuela, while other major oil companies remain wary after having assets nationalized under Hugo Chávez. The deal is part of a broader U.S. effort to reopen Venezuela's oil industry to foreign investment following the January U.S. military operation that removed Nicolás Maduro and installed Delcy Rodríguez as interim president. Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-venezuela-oil-u-s-majority-control-65-billion-barrels/

headline: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is considering bringing hundreds of senior military leaders back to Marine Corps Base Quantico for another address later this year, according to U.S. officials. Hegseth held a similar meeting there last September, when he summoned generals and admirals on short notice to outline his priorities for the force. The event focused heavily on warfighting, physical and grooming standards, and reversing diversity and inclusion policies from the previous administration. Officials say a second Quantico meeting would likely be used to outline additional priorities and issue new directives, although the date and exact attendance have not been determined. The Pentagon says it has nothing to announce at this time. It also remains unclear whether President Trump would attend, as he did last year. The potential meeting comes as Hegseth continues efforts to reshape military policies around physical standards, appearance and what he describes as a renewed focus on warfighting. headline: Federal authorities are preparing potential charges against a U.S. servicemember accused of making more than $1 million in profits from Polymarket bets tied to military operations, according to people familiar with the investigation. The servicemember, who has been under scrutiny since the spring, allegedly made successful bets involving the timing or outcomes of U.S. military strikes in Iran and Venezuela. The case is part of a broader federal investigation into whether military personnel used confidential information to trade prediction-market contracts. A separate investigation involves a KPMG employee accused of betting on whether a public company would beat quarterly earnings expectations, potentially using nonpublic information obtained through their employment. Charges in both cases could come this fall, although prosecutors have not made final decisions. The investigations involve the Justice Department, federal prosecutors in Manhattan and Washington, and the CFTC. The cases are part of a broader effort to determine how existing insider-trading and financial-fraud laws apply to prediction markets such as Polymarket. Previous prosecutions involving alleged insider trading on the platform are already facing challenges over whether those laws apply to prediction-market contracts. Notably, the servicemember has not been charged at this point. The allegations remain under investigation. headline: The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has released its preliminary report into the loss of separation incident involving a U.S. Marine Corps VH-3D operating as Marine One and a passenger aircraft departing Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) on August 4. The incident occurred as Marine One departed the temporary landing zone at the Ellipse, carrying President Donald J. Trump to Joint Base Andrews for his flight to the West Coast. According to the preliminary report, Marine One twice attempted to contact DCA Tower, advising controllers that the helicopter was approximately three minutes from liftoff. The calls appear to have been intended to give air traffic control advance notice so departing traffic could be stopped or otherwise managed as necessary. Approximately three minutes after the initial notification, Marine One contacted the tower again, advising that it was proceeding as briefed. The controller then advised the helicopter of departing traffic and instructed the aircraft to go around, climb and turn away from the traffic.
